extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Latin literature / classical studies (readers of Horace)
extracted.subtask_description: Annotated edition and commentary on Horace's Satires (translations, textual notes, and explanatory commentary). Includes Latin text with line numbers, variant readings, glosses, and interpretive summaries aimed at understanding language, allusions, and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record manuscript variants and editorial emendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Show and discuss variant readings from manuscripts and the emendations proposed by editors (e.g., Bentley, Orelli, Wickham, Lejay); indicate words that can be deleted or altered in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The apparatus and notes give examples: "^ quam rem Bentley : mss, show quas res, which can be kept if tibi or agis is deleted. Thus Orelli, Wickham, Lejay." — record the variants, the editor who proposes them, and the rationale (e.g., deletion of a word). Use sigla and footnotes to track readings and conjectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve original Latin text with line numbers and present a facing/paraphrase translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the Latin lines (numbered) and an English rendering or paraphrase immediately adjacent so readers can follow the sense and structure of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This edition interleaves Latin lines (with numbers) and an English rendering (e.g., Latin lines 20-40 followed by English paraphrase). Keep lineation and numbering to facilitate reference and commentary; note where translations are interpretive rather than strictly literal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide glosses and lexical explanations for difficult or colloquial usages
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain unusual, archaic, or colloquial words and constructions (e.g., colloquial use of 'noster' = 'I').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply short glosses and notes in the apparatus: "^ This colloquial use of noster ='I', for which we have examples in Plautus..." and give cross-references or comparative examples to justify the gloss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotate cultural, historical, and mythological references
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and explain references to Roman institutions, gods, customs, people, and events (e.g., Janus, Maecenas, praetor's tribunal, Saturnalia, Pythagoras' prohibition on beans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concise explanatory notes and citations: e.g., "The praetor's tribunal was near the Puteal Libonis...", "During the Saturnalia slaves were allowed great freedom"; where helpful cite parallel passages (Sat. i.8.14) or ancient sources (Gellius).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain literary tone, devices, and rhetorical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss the poem's tone and figures (e.g., 'mock heroic', apostrophe, dramatic dialogue) and how they function in the passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit commentary such as: "The language is mock heroic, and the apostrophe of the god of the morn... indicates the time of day when Horace was writing." Analyze dramatic form (dialogue, satire), humour, Stoic paradoxes, and how these shape meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize argument, structure, and thematic content
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide concise synopses of scenes, speaker roles, and the poem's themes (e.g., freedom of the wise, contrast master/slave, city vs country).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer section summaries and thematic statements as in the introduction: "The scene is laid in Rome during the Saturnalia... Davus remarks that some men are consistent in their vices... Who, then, is free? Only the wise man..." Use these summaries to orient readers before or after close readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-reference parallel passages and scholarly authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate lines and motifs to other passages in Horace or other classical authors and cite modern editors/commentators (e.g., references to Lucretius, Milton, Bentley, Lejay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include parenthetical references and notes: e.g., "Cf. Milton's 'Or hear'st thou rather pure ethereal stream' {Par. Lost, iii. 6}", "The expression is probably an echo of Lucretius (i. 717)". Cite prior scholarship when suggesting readings or interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply textual and interpretive notes to resolve contextual or cultural ambiguities
rubrics_metrics.description: Where meanings, customs, or referents are uncertain, present plausible explanations, alternatives, or conjectures, with rationale and levels of confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the notes: "The expression used for Sicily is probably an echo of Lucretius..."; "Another plausible interpretation of libatis dapibus is 'after due offering'..." Mark conjectures and variants clearly, and indicate when readings are uncertain or contested.
